title: Conclusion
text: Delivery time on Olist is driven mainly by route: where the seller is, where the customer is, and whether the two are in the same state. Product and order characteristics add a smaller amount, and purchase timing adds very little beyond a few slow months. The best model (Decision Tree on R3 + Olist estimate) predicts delivery time on unseen orders to within about 4.8 days on average and explains about 31% of the variation, using only information available at checkout. That is 24% lower error than always predicting the average (6.3 days), and 9% lower than the first-draft model (5.2 days), which used fewer features and was scored on a split that did not keep orders together. Olist’s own checkout estimate is much looser: on its own it explains only 15% of the variation, and on the test orders it is on average 11.5 days longer than what actually happened. What follows turns those findings into concrete order scenarios and recommendations.

# Brazil's five macro-regions, used to group destination states into service tiers
macro_region <- function(state) {
  case_when(
    state %in% c("AC", "AM", "AP", "PA", "RO", "RR", "TO") ~ "North",
    state %in% c("AL", "BA", "CE", "MA", "PB", "PE", "PI", "RN", "SE") ~ "Northeast",
    state %in% c("DF", "GO", "MS", "MT") ~ "Center-West",
    state %in% c("ES", "MG", "RJ", "SP") ~ "Southeast",
    state %in% c("PR", "RS", "SC") ~ "South",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )
}

tier_levels <- c("Same state", "Cross-state to Southeast", "Cross-state to South",
                 "Cross-state to Center-West", "Cross-state to Northeast",
                 "Cross-state to North")

tp <- test_preds |>
  mutate(
    route_tier = if_else(
      same_state == "same", "Same state",
      paste0("Cross-state to ", macro_region(as.character(customer_state)))
    ),
    route_tier = factor(route_tier, levels = tier_levels)
  )

# For each tier: promise vs. actual, plus the 10th and 90th percentile of the residual

  group_by(route_tier) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    actual = mean(delivery_days),
    olist = mean(estimated_days),
    padding = mean(estimated_days - delivery_days),
    olist_late = mean(delivery_days > estimated_days),

text:
Six order scenarios, predicted
To make the model concrete, we score six “typical order” profiles. For each one we take real training orders on that route (seller state to customer state), use their median freight, weight, price, size, and Olist estimate, and set the purchase month. August is a fast month in the exploration, and November is a slow one. Both the lasso (the interpretable linear model) and the decision tree (the most accurate model) score each profile.


Code
# Most common category among a route's orders
mode_level <- function(x) {
  tab <- table(as.character(x))
  x[which(as.character(x) == names(which.max(tab)))[1]]
}

# A "typical order" on a route: median values for numeric fields and the most common
# category for the rest, taken from real training orders, with the purchase month set explicitly
build_scenario <- function(label, seller, cust, month) {
  rows <- train |> filter(seller_state == seller, customer_state == cust)
  stopifnot(nrow(rows) > 0)

  rows |>
    summarise(
      across(where(is.numeric), \(x) median(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      across(where(is.factor), mode_level)
    ) |>
    select(-delivery_days) |>
    mutate(
      order_id = "scenario",
      purchase_month = factor(as.character(month), levels = levels(train$purchase_month)),
      label = label,
      n_similar = nrow(rows),
      route_median_days = median(rows$delivery_days)
    )
}

title: Conclusion
text:
What the team should do

Make the delivery promise route-aware. Set the checkout estimate from seller state, customer state, and month, instead of one rule for everything. The tier table shows how unevenly the current estimate is padded (9.9 days on Same state, 16 days on Cross-state to North). A pilot of a route-aware promise on a few routes would show how many days could be saved without raising the late rate. Measure it by: average promised days and the late rate, by route tier.
Show a delivery window, not a single date. Point predictions are good on average but miss the slow tail, and the width of the uncertainty depends on the route (about 9 days on the tightest tier and 23 days on Cross-state to North, measured as the middle 80% of outcomes). Offering “between day X and day Y” is more honest and matches how the model behaves. Measure it by: the share of orders that land inside the window, which should be close to the 80% it is designed for.
Add a seasonal buffer for the slow months. Orders placed in Mar, Nov, Feb are late most often. Extend the promise or add carrier capacity in those months. Check whether the pattern holds in newer data before committing. Measure it by: the late rate in those months, year over year.
Treat the north and northeast as a separate service tier. Routes into these regions are the slowest and the hardest to predict (the highest-error tier is Cross-state to North, with an average miss of 8 days). Set separate expectations, review carrier performance on these lanes, and consider whether stocking inventory closer to these customers is worth testing. Measure it by: delivery time and prediction error on these lanes, tracked separately.
Test whether sourcing closer to the buyer helps. Same-state routes are the fastest and the single most-used feature in the tree. That is an association, not proof that moving a seller would change delivery time, because sellers and buyers in the same state may also differ in carrier mix and product type. A small pilot, such as a “ships from your state” badge or search ranking, would show whether the effect is real. Measure it by: conversion and delivery time on the pilot group against a control.
Do not spend effort on purchase weekday, time of day, or listing quality. Weekday and time of day barely moved delivery outcomes in the exploration, and listing-quality fields added nothing visible to the models. Put effort into route, carrier, and seller handling instead.
Look at seller handling time. The shipping deadline the seller was given (ship_window_days) is one of the more-used features in the tree. We cannot tell from this data whether sellers who are given more time actually take more time, so this is a question to investigate with seller-level shipping timestamps.
Keep the model honest over time. Retrain on recent orders at a regular interval, watch average error by route tier, and treat a sustained rise in error as a sign that carrier performance or demand has shifted.

title: Conclusion
text:
How far to trust it

Accuracy is useful, not exact. A typical miss is about 4.8 days, and the average error is much smaller than the error on the worst orders (RMSE 7.6 days). This is good for checkout windows and capacity planning, not for day-exact commitments.
The slow tail is still hard. The model under-predicts the slowest orders, because it predicts a typical value for a right-skewed target. That is why we recommend a window with a buffer.
A random split tests similar orders, not future ones. The test orders come from the same 2016 to 2018 period as the training orders. The model has not been tested on a new carrier contract, a strike, or a different year.
Single test set. Differences of a few hundredths of a day between models are not meaningful.
Order-item grain. delivery_days is an order-level duration repeated across the items of an order, so multi-item orders carry slightly more weight in the metrics.
Associations, not causes. The importance scores and coefficients show what the models rely on to predict. They do not show what causes a delay, which is why recommendations 5 and 7 are framed as tests.
Coarse geography. Zip-code region is only a rough stand-in for distance, and the scenarios use median values for each route.

title: Conclusion
text:
What would improve it next

Real seller-to-customer distance from Olist’s geolocation table, which is the most promising feature not yet used.
Stage-level timestamps (approval, handoff to carrier, delivery), so seller handling time and carrier transit time can be modelled separately and each team can see its own share.
A time-based test: train on earlier months and test on later ones, which is a stricter check than a random split.
Non-linear ensemble models and a log-transformed target. Earlier experiments suggested these can lower typical error, at the cost of being harder to explain.

text:
Decision, Limitations, and Next Steps (Milestone 2)
Adopt route- and weight-aware delivery buffers rather than a single flat delivery promise—for example, accounting for multi-week differences between SP (8.3 mean customer days) and distant states such as RR (27.8 mean days), as well as heavier 10kg+ shipments (14.9 mean days)
### Limitations Historical scope & missing timestamps: The Olist dataset covers 2016–2018 operations and omits orders lacking recorded delivery dates, so estimates may not reflect current carrier routing or unfulfilled orders. Small counts in remote states & non-predictive outcome fields: Low order counts in remote states increase variance of raw averages, and post-delivery fields (delayed_days, delivered_status) are excluded from feature exploration to avoid leakage.

title: Home
text:
Why this matters
Olist is a Brazilian online marketplace that connects small sellers to customers across the country. Delivery speed and shipping cost are central to customer satisfaction, and they are set by logistics: where the seller and customer are, how heavy the item is, and what category it belongs to. About two years of order data (2016-2018) can show where the delivery promise holds, where it breaks, and what drives shipping costs.
Use the navbar: Data and Exploration are the analysis, covering the order-level dataset (about 110K item rows), the calculated fields I built (delivery status, total cost, time-of-day features), and the plots that compare delivery time, freight, weight, and category. The remaining pages cover the file format, the presentation slides, and the GitHub and Netlify setup.

title: Home
text:
What I found so far

About 90% of orders arrive earlier than estimated, so Olist’s delivery estimates are conservative.
Purchase timing (weekday vs. weekend, time of day) barely changes delivery outcomes.
Location and product type matter more: delivery time varies by customer state and by category, and heavier items cost more to ship.

Summary of Cleaning Decisions (One Sentence per Rule)

Column name & date standardization: Corrected the raw typos (product_name_lenght -> product_name_length and product_description_lenght -> product_description_length) and built purchase_year_month so naming is consistent and monthly trends can be tracked cleanly.
Missing target removal: Removed 2,454 rows (2.18%) missing delivery_days—moving from 112,650 to 110,196 rows—because records without an observed delivery duration cannot train or evaluate a delivery_days model.
Category missingness ("unknown"): Filled missing product_category_name and product_category_name_english entries with "unknown" rather than dropping rows so uncategorized items still contribute shipping, timing, and geographic records.
Numeric product spec imputation (median): Imputed missing values across the seven numeric product specification columns (product_name_length, product_description_length, product_photos_qty, product_weight_g, product_length_cm, product_height_cm, and product_width_cm) using each column’s median because product dimensions and counts are skewed and the median resists extreme outliers.

Saves the cleaned df_master dataset to data/df_master_clean.rds so downstream pages load a consistent, validated dataset.

title: Modeling
text:
This analysis builds models that predict delivery_days (days from order purchase to customer delivery) using only information that is available when an order is placed or approved. It starts from the cleaned order-item dataset prepared on the Data page, engineers route, product, and timing features, and compares three feature recipes across four model families, plus benchmarks, on a held-out test set.
Design choices

Split by order, not by row. The data has one row per order item, and delivery_days repeats across the items of an order. If items from one order landed in both training and test data, the test score would be inflated. Every split below keeps all items of an order together.
Train / validation / test, no cross-validation. Model settings are chosen on a validation set carved out of the training data. The test set is used once, at the end.
Three recipes that add one group of features at a time, so we can see what each group contributes.
Four model families: linear regression, ridge, lasso, and a decision tree.
Metrics in days. We keep delivery_days on its raw scale so errors are directly interpretable. MAE (average absolute error) is the primary metric, RMSE (which penalizes large misses more) is secondary, and R² is the traditional version, 1 - SSE/SST on the test set. An R² of 0 means no better than predicting the average; it can be negative.

We build features in four groups: route (where the item travels), timing, product and order characteristics, and Olist’s own checkout estimate.

  # Order size: how many items, and how many different sellers, share one order
  group_by(order_id) |>
  mutate(n_items = n(), n_sellers = n_distinct(seller_id)) |>
  ungroup() |>

make_recipe <- function(preds) {
  rec <- recipe(delivery_days ~ .,
                data = train |> select(delivery_days, order_id, all_of(preds))) |>
    # order_id only identifies the order; it is not a predictor
    update_role(order_id, new_role = "id") |>
    # A category first seen after training gets its own level instead of causing an error
    step_novel(all_nominal_predictors())
  # Rare product categories (under 1% of rows) are pooled; states are deliberately not pooled
  # because the smallest states are the slowest destinations
  if ("category" %in% preds) rec <- rec |> step_other(category, threshold = 0.01)
  rec |>
    # Each category becomes a 0/1 indicator column
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    # Drop constant columns, and columns that duplicate other columns exactly
    step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_lincomb(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    # Put every numeric predictor on the same scale so penalties treat them evenly
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
}

Benchmarks give the models something to beat:

Naive: always predict the average training delivery time.
Olist estimate only: a one-variable linear model on estimated_days.
First-draft ridge: the ridge model from the project’s first modeling iteration (freight, weight, state, and purchase month), refit on the same grouped split so the comparison is fair.

Models: linear regression (no settings), ridge and lasso (one setting each, the penalty), and a decision tree (depth and minimum node size). The penalty and tree settings are chosen as follows: fit each candidate on the training sub-sample, measure MAE on the validation set, and keep the candidate with the lowest validation MAE. The chosen settings are then refit on the full training data and scored once on the test set.


Code
# Metrics: RMSE and MAE in days, and traditional R-squared (1 - SSE/SST)
mset <- metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq_trad)

fit_wf <- function(rec, spec, data) {
  workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(spec) |> fit(data)
}
# Average absolute error in days on a dataset; used to compare candidate settings
mae_on <- function(fit, data) {
  predict(fit, new_data = data) |>
    bind_cols(data |> select(delivery_days)) |>
    mae(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred) |>
    pull(.estimate)
}
score_fit <- function(fit) {
  predict(fit, new_data = test) |>
    bind_cols(test |> select(delivery_days)) |>
    mset(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred)
}

glmnet_spec <- function(p, mixture) {
  linear_reg(penalty = p, mixture = mixture) |> set_engine("glmnet")
}
# cost_complexity is fixed at a small value, so depth and minimum node size control tree complexity
tree_spec <- function(d, m) {
  decision_tree(tree_depth = d, min_n = m, cost_complexity = 0.0001) |>
    set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("regression")
}

# Candidate settings: penalties from very weak (1e-5) to strong (1), and six tree shapes
pen_grid  <- 10^seq(-5, 0, length.out = 10)
tree_grid <- expand_grid(tree_depth = c(5, 8, 12), min_n = c(20, 60))

# Fit each candidate on the training sub-sample and keep the one with the lowest validation MAE
tune_pen <- function(rec, mixture) {
  maes <- map_dbl(pen_grid, \(p) fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(p, mixture), train_sub) |> mae_on(val))
  pen_grid[which.min(maes)]
}
tune_tree <- function(rec) {
  maes <- pmap_dbl(tree_grid, \(tree_depth, min_n)
                   fit_wf(rec, tree_spec(tree_depth, min_n), train_sub) |> mae_on(val))
  tree_grid[which.min(maes), ]
}

The same procedure is applied to each of the three recipes, giving twelve final models (four model families on three recipes) plus the three benchmarks.


Code
cache_file <- "data/modeling_cache.rds"

if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  cache <- read_rds(cache_file)
} else {
  # Benchmarks: simple reference points that every model has to beat
  bench_naive <- test |>
    mutate(.pred = mean(train$delivery_days)) |>
    mset(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "Naive (train mean)", settings = "")

  fit_olist <- fit_wf(recipe(delivery_days ~ estimated_days, data = train),
                      linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"), train)
  bench_olist <- score_fit(fit_olist) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "Olist estimate only (LM)", settings = "")

  # First-draft model: the original small feature set, refit on the same grouped split
  rec_orig <- recipe(delivery_days ~ freight_value + product_weight_g +
                       customer_state + seller_state + purchase_month,
                     data = train) |>
    step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.02) |>
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
  fit_orig <- fit_wf(rec_orig, glmnet_spec(0.1, 0), train)
  bench_orig <- score_fit(fit_orig) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "First-draft ridge (original features)",
           settings = "penalty=0.1")

  # Fit all four model families on each recipe. Settings are chosen on the validation set,
  # then the final models are refit on the full training data
  run_recipe <- function(preds, rec_name) {
    rec   <- make_recipe(preds)
    pen_r <- tune_pen(rec, 0)
    pen_l <- tune_pen(rec, 1)
    bt    <- tune_tree(rec)

    fits <- list(
      "Linear Regression" = fit_wf(rec, linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"), train),
      "Ridge"             = fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(pen_r, 0), train),
      "Lasso"             = fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(pen_l, 1), train),
      "Decision Tree"     = fit_wf(rec, tree_spec(bt$tree_depth, bt$min_n), train)
    )
    settings <- c(
      "Linear Regression" = "none",
      "Ridge"             = paste0("penalty=", signif(pen_r, 2)),
      "Lasso"             = paste0("penalty=", signif(pen_l, 2)),
      "Decision Tree"     = paste0("depth=", bt$tree_depth, ", min_n=", bt$min_n)
    )

    list(
      metrics = imap(fits, \(fit, model_name)
                     score_fit(fit) |>
                       mutate(recipe = rec_name, model = model_name,
                              settings = settings[[model_name]])) |>
        list_rbind(),
      fits = fits[c("Lasso", "Decision Tree")]
    )
  }

  runs <- imap(recipe_defs, run_recipe)

  cache <- list(
    results_all = bind_rows(bench_naive, bench_olist, bench_orig,
                            map(runs, "metrics") |> list_rbind()),
    fit_lasso3  = runs[["R3 + Olist estimate"]]$fits[["Lasso"]],
    fit_tree3   = runs[["R3 + Olist estimate"]]$fits[["Decision Tree"]]
  )
  write_rds(cache, cache_file)
}

title: Modeling
text:
Each recipe adds one group of predictors to the previous one. Comparing them shows what each group is worth.


Code
# Predictor groups. Each recipe adds one group to the one before it, so the
# improvement from each group of features can be measured on its own
preds_geo <- c("customer_state", "seller_state", "same_state", "cust_region",
               "seller_region", "same_region", "purchase_year",
               "purchase_month", "purchase_dow")

preds_prod <- c("freight_value", "price", "freight_ratio", "product_weight_g",
                "volume_cm3", "density_g_cm3", "n_items", "n_sellers",
                "ship_window_days", "category", "product_photos_qty",
                "product_name_length", "product_description_length")

recipe_defs <- list(
  "R1 Geography + timing" = preds_geo,
  "R2 + Product & order"  = c(preds_geo, preds_prod),
  "R3 + Olist estimate"   = c(preds_geo, preds_prod, "estimated_days")
)

make_recipe <- function(preds) {
  rec <- recipe(delivery_days ~ .,
                data = train |> select(delivery_days, order_id, all_of(preds))) |>
    # order_id only identifies the order; it is not a predictor
    update_role(order_id, new_role = "id") |>
    # A category first seen after training gets its own level instead of causing an error
    step_novel(all_nominal_predictors())
  # Rare product categories (under 1% of rows) are pooled; states are deliberately not pooled
  # because the smallest states are the slowest destinations
  if ("category" %in% preds) rec <- rec |> step_other(category, threshold = 0.01)
  rec |>
    # Each category becomes a 0/1 indicator column
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    # Drop constant columns, and columns that duplicate other columns exactly
    step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_lincomb(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    # Put every numeric predictor on the same scale so penalties treat them evenly
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
}

  Recipe = names(recipe_defs),
  `Predictors (n)` = map_int(recipe_defs, length),

    "R1 plus freight, price, weight, volume, density, order size, ship window, product category, listing quality",

Test MAE by recipe and model; the dashed line is the Olist-estimate-only benchmark







Best configuration: Decision Tree on R3 + Olist estimate, with a test MAE of 4.79 days, RMSE of 7.61 days, and R² of 0.31. In plain terms, using only information available at checkout, the model explains about 31% of the variation in delivery time, with a typical miss of about 4.8 days.
Improvement over the benchmarks: MAE is 24% lower than always predicting the average (6.31 days), and 9% lower than the first-draft ridge (5.25 days; R² 0.24) on the same grouped split.
Features matter more than model choice. For linear regression, adding product and order features (R1 to R2) lowers MAE from 5.01 to 4.87 days. Adding Olist’s own estimate (R2 to R3) lowers it only to 4.85 days. That estimate is weak on its own (R² of 0.15), and most of what it knows about the route is already captured by the state and region features.
Regularization made almost no difference. In Recipe 3, linear regression, ridge, and lasso have RMSEs between 7.59 and 7.6 days. With about 88,157 training rows and a modest number of predictors, there is little overfitting for a penalty to fix. Differences this small are within the noise of a single test split.
The tree is close to the linear models, not far ahead. In Recipe 3 the decision tree’s MAE is 4.79 days against 4.85 for linear regression, a gap of 0.06 days. Its RMSE (7.61) is slightly worse than linear regression’s (7.59), which suggests the tree does not handle the longest delays any better.
RMSE is much larger than MAE (7.6 vs 4.8 days): most orders are predicted well, but a minority of very late orders produce large errors. The diagnostics below look at this directly.

title: Modeling
text:
The lasso shrinks the coefficients of unhelpful predictors to exactly zero, so the features that survive are the ones the model finds useful. Predictors are standardized, so each coefficient is the change in predicted delivery days for a one-standard-deviation increase in that predictor (for a dummy variable, a one-standard-deviation change in the 0/1 indicator). Coefficients show direction and relative size, not causal effects.


Code
# Coefficients are per one standard deviation of each predictor; zero means the lasso dropped it
lasso_coefs <- tidy(fit_lasso3) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)")
n_kept  <- sum(lasso_coefs$estimate != 0)
n_total <- nrow(lasso_coefs)

top_coefs <- lasso_coefs |>
  filter(estimate != 0) |>
  slice_max(abs(estimate), n = 15) |>
  mutate(direction = if_else(estimate > 0, "Slower delivery", "Faster delivery"))

  geom_col() +

Largest lasso coefficients (Recipe 3, standardized predictors)




The lasso kept 109 of 112 encoded predictors.



A tree’s raw importance scores are split across dummy columns, so a feature like customer_state appears as 27 small bars. We add the scores back together by original feature to get a clearer picture.


Code
imp <- extract_fit_engine(fit_tree3)$variable.importance

imp_tbl <- tibble(term = names(imp), importance = imp) |>
  # A feature such as customer_state is split into many dummy columns; add them back together
  mutate(feature = case_when(
    str_detect(term, "^customer_state") ~ "customer_state",
    str_detect(term, "^seller_state")   ~ "seller_state",
    str_detect(term, "^same_state")     ~ "same_state",
    str_detect(term, "^same_region")    ~ "same_region",
    str_detect(term, "^cust_region")    ~ "customer_zip_region",
    str_detect(term, "^seller_region")  ~ "seller_zip_region",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_year")  ~ "purchase_year",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_month") ~ "purchase_month",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_dow")   ~ "purchase_weekday",
    str_detect(term, "^category")       ~ "product_category",
    TRUE ~ term
  )) |>
  group_by(feature) |>
  summarise(importance = sum(importance), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share = importance / sum(importance)) |>
  arrange(desc(importance))

imp_tbl |>
  slice_head(n = 12) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = reorder(feature, share))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2b8cbe") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Decision tree: share of importance by feature (Recipe 3)",
    x = "Share of total importance", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()





Decision tree importance, summed across dummy columns (Recipe 3)








Route features dominate. The three most important feature groups in the tree are customer_state (18%), same_state (17%), and estimated_days (14%). Where an item travels from and to is the strongest driver of delivery time.
Purchase timing contributes a smaller share (10% for year, month, and weekday combined), consistent with the exploration page’s finding that purchase timing barely changes delivery outcomes. The months that do show up match the slow months seen in the exploration.
estimated_days ranks high in importance but added little to accuracy. The tree uses it often, but because route features carry much of the same information, removing it costs little. Importance measures how much a feature is used; the recipe comparison measures how much accuracy it adds.
Caution: correlated features share credit in tree importance, and neither the lasso nor the tree shows causation. These results describe what the models rely on to predict, not what causes a delay.
